narr: Debby first developed into a tropical storm about 100 miles west-southwest of Key West, Florida late afternoon on August 3rd, then gradually strengthened to a strong tropical storm while tracking north across the eastern Gulf of Mexico on August 4th. Debby then reached hurricane force strength late on August 4th about 100 miles west-northwest of Tampa, before continuing a north-northeast track across the eastern Gulf of Mexico and eventually making landfall near the Big Bend area of Florida as a Category 1 Hurricane during the morning of August 5th. Debby continued inland and weakened to a tropical storm while tracking northeast across northern Florida later on August 5th, then continued a gradual weakening trend while tracking across Southeast Georgia as a tropical storm (45 mph) before slowly emerging off the Southeast Coast at tropical storm strength (40 mph) near Tybee Island, Georgia on August 6th. Debby then tracked east and farther offshore early August 7th, then turned north and became a strong tropical storm (60 mph) over the Gulf Stream later that morning, before taking a more north-northwest track back toward the Southeast Coast and making landfall near Awendaw/Bulls Bay, South Carolina as a tropical storm (50 mph) around 2 AM on August 8th. A minimum surface pressure of 994 mb was recorded at Sullivan���s Island (XSLV), South Carolina prior to Debby making landfall. After landfall, Debby continued on a north-northwest track across South Carolina as a tropical storm into mid day August 8th, before weakening to a depression later that day and continuing a north path across North Carolina and Virginia into early August 9th. ||Across Southeast South Carolina, the main impacts associated with Debby included flash flooding due to widespread heavy rainfall, several nighttime tornadoes within rainbands and scattered tree damage associated with near tropical storm force winds. ||Prolonged heavy rainfall across Southeast South Carolina brought widespread flash flooding on August 5th and 6th, additional areas of flash flooding on August 7th, 8th and 9th, along with considerable and prolonged flooding of creeks, streams and main stem rivers for several days thereafter. Numerous homes and roads were flooded, leading to rescues and/or evacuations. Storm total rainfall amounts from August 4th to August 9th generally ranged between 4 to 22 inches with highest amounts across the Quad County Area (Berkeley, Dorchester, Charleston, Colleton) and particularly along a stretch from Summerville, Ridgeville, St George and Harleyville, South Carolina to Moncks Corner, South Carolina. A peak storm total rainfall of 22.02 inches was recorded by a CoCoRaHS observer approximately 6.6 miles southwest of Moncks Corner, South Carolina. A daily record rainfall of 4.71 inches was also set on August 6th at the Charleston International Airport (KCHS). Despite a large amount of rain and flash flooding, storm surge/coastal flooding did not lead to mentionable impacts locally. The highest water level at the Charleston (CHTS1) tide gauge was 1.06 ft MHHW during the evening of August 5th. No injuries or fatalities occurred with flash flooding/flooding.||Several rainbands associated with Debby brought 8 tornadoes (4 EF1 and 4 EF0) across coastal counties of Southeast South Carolina during the night of August 5th into early August 6th, causing damage to numerous trees and many structures. An EF1 tornado in Berkeley County caused 2 minor injuries when a car was flipped by the tornado. A total of 2 minor injuries and no fatalities occurred with tornadoes. ||Tropical storm force winds/gusts produced scattered tree damage and communication/power outages across several counties. One minor injury occurred when a tree fell down on a vehicle in Beaufort County, South Carolina. Strongest winds were recorded across coastal areas and nearby coastal waters. The highest sustained tropical storm wind (39 knots) and highest tropical storm wind gust (55 knots) occurred at Folly Beach South End (XFSE), South Carolina. Across nearby coastal waters, the highest sustained tropical storm wind (44 knots) and highest tropical storm wind gust (51 knots) occurred at the Edisto Buoy (41004). A total of 1 minor injury and no fatalities occurred by tropical cyclone winds.
ev: A NWS employee reported that flood waters entered several businesses along Ashley River Road near Otis Avenue.
A Colleton County emergency manager reported Bennetts Point Road near the intersection with Island Flats Lane closed due to deep flooding. The entire area was impassable.
A video posted on social media shows water rapidly flowing across a commercial parking lot and across a boat ramp near Reid Hill Road.
Law enforcement reported a road washed out near the intersection of Cane Branch Road and Edward Road.
Firefighters located at Charleston Fire Station 8 on Huger Street reported several inches of floodwater entering the station Tuesday morning.
Emergency officials in Moncks Corner reported that high water rescues were in progress, homes were flooded throughout the city and roads were closed due to 2-3 feet of fast moving water.

A Dorchester County emergency manager and media reported at least 75 roads closed due to flooding across Dorchester County this morning. A slightly larger amount of road closures were near Harleyville, Summerville and along the Edisto River.
A Dorchester County emergency manager shared a picture of a washout along the paved 695 Block of Powder Horn Road.
Dorchester County Emergency Management reported that the Department of Transportation was shutting down Delmar Highway at Ashley Ridge High School because floodwaters were washing the roadway away.
Berkeley County Emergency Management reported Heatly Street in Moncks Corner being closed due to high water caused by flash flooding.
A video posted on social media showed two dikes at Crosbys Pond breached due to heavy rainfall and all water in the 20 acre pond rapidly draining into nearby Black Creek.
Law enforcement reported flood waters entering through the front door of a home along Broughton Circle.
A NWS employee reported water entering the back of several homes near Ashley Hall Road and St Julian Drive.
The water level on Church Creek near West Ashley was 6.51 ft and rising. Moderate flood stage is 6.5 ft. At 6.5 ft, water from the creek commonly impacts Crosstowne Church.
Law enforcement reported a portion of roadway damaged in the 2500 Block of Black Creek Road.
Law enforcement reported a portion of roadway damaged near the intersection of Black Creek Road and Edward Road.

Law enforcement reported a portion of roadway damaged in the 100 Block of Good Hope Landing Lane.
The public reported flowing water entering buildings near the intersection of Furman Lane and Oxford Road.

The City of Charleston reported over 60 roads closed across the city due to flooding. The City of Charleston web page indicated that all primary access points to the Charleston Peninsula were closed to incoming traffic due to widespread flooding.
Berkeley County Emergency Management reported a washout of Cane Gulley Road near Highway 402.
Law enforcement reported a portion of roadway washed out in the 600 Block of Wiggins Road.

Law enforcement reported a portion of roadway washed out in the 400 Block of Paradise Road.
Jasper County Emergency Management reported Langfordville Road collapsed over Beaverdam Branch, washing a car and occupant downstream. An adult female was rescued from the floodwaters without injury.

The public relayed a video of a flooded house on Fairlawn Drive in Moncks Corner.

Colleton County Emergency Management reported a road washout at 5000 Wiggins Road.
Law enforcement reported a portion of roadway damaged in the 2400 Block of Mewville Road.

A Dorchester County emergency manager relayed an image of water moving over Salem Road where it intersects with Halfway Gut Creek.
Berkeley County Emergency Management reported approximately 30 swift water rescues within Berkeley County, mainly in Moncks Corner. No injuries have been reported.

A Colleton County emergency manager reported Charleston Highway closed due to flooding at Horseshoe Creek Bridge between Neyles and Jacksonboro, South Carolina. Water was actively flowing over the roadway.
